PlayBook2023–24Startup · creator platform

Turn creator rules into fan experiences.

Creators define campaigns and item rules in Studio; fans participate, collect and craft in the App. I connected the interaction logic between these two sides.

Problem
Creators can configure crafting rules freely in Studio. The more freedom they have, the harder it is for creators and fans to see how a rule actually works.
Key decisions
I made the rule a set of blocks you can handle on a canvas rather than a form; arranged the five parallel views in the requirements into the order a fan moves through on one visit; and argued that everyday progress and major rewards should not get equally intrusive feedback, so minor progress no longer opens a full-screen dialog.
Outcome
The client’s founder used the interactive prototypes in investor pitches, and the project secured investment.
Context
Startup · Creator & fan platform
My role
Studio UX/UI · App UX
Period
2023–2024
Delivery
Flows, interfaces, states & prototypes

01 · Product model

One rule connects the creator and the fan.

PlayBook aimed to keep the relationship between creators and fans continuous across content platforms. Tasks, collectible items and crafting rules offered ways for fans to express participation. The product needed to complement existing channels and lead people back to the creator’s content.

I designed Studio’s UX and UI, alongside the App’s UX flows and interaction states. Another designer created the App’s visual UI. Both sides shared a core challenge: a freely configured rule must become understandable when someone uses it.

Studio

Configure

Creators organise campaigns, tasks, items and crafting rules.

App

Participate

Fans find tasks in a creator’s community and acquire items.

Community

Express connection

Collecting, using and displaying items reflects the relationship with the creator.

02 · Users & flow

Fans open the app to see what they have just earned.

The client’s requirements listed nine reasons a fan would open PlayBook. The first was to check what they had earned after engaging with a creator on social media. The rest fell into three groups: following activity, managing a collection, and interacting with creators and other fans.

I worked from three user types across the two sides of the product. On the fan side, I talked with viewers of virtual streamers about why they watch and what draws them in, combined that with my own experience as a livestream viewer, and wrote two personas: the long-time supporter and the newcomer. What I knew about creators came from the client’s conversations with creators and their agencies.

The requirements described the app as five parallel views: Home, Missions, Crafting, Inventory and Community. I arranged them in the order a fan moves through on one visit: see rewards and open missions on Home, complete missions (some on the original platform), claim items, check what is missing in the catalogue, craft, trade or swap, and finally show items off.

Tobie’s note

New fans don’t yet know which items are valuable. That cold-start problem turned the showcase from self-curated into recommended, one-tap display.

Fan · long-time supporter

Follows a creator across platforms

Watches streams, follows the creator’s social accounts and buys merchandise. When the creator moves to a new main platform, past badges and levels disappear, and long-term support often goes unnoticed. Needs contributions to be kept and visible.

Fan · newcomer

A new fan who likes collecting

Has just started following a creator and is drawn to rare items and events. Beyond likes and comments there is little to do, and they don’t yet know which items are valuable. Needs to know what to do today, what is missing and where to get it.

Creator · Studio

A VTuber with a character and a story

Builds an audience across YouTube, Twitch and other platforms, loses many fans when switching main platform, and can’t easily see who the long-term supporters are. Needs to turn missions, items, recipes and campaigns into rules fans can understand.

03 · Studio

Show the logic while the rule is being edited.

The rule editor places required inputs, optional inputs, conditional branches and outputs on one canvas. In the source example, a gamepad and battery are required, while a supercharger is optional. Selecting it changes how an output attribute is calculated.

This structure makes the relationship between inputs and outcomes traceable. Its trade-off is canvas complexity: greater flexibility makes it more important to test whether first-time creators can find the entry point, explain their rule and correct mistakes.

Free to play with

Build a crafting recipe yourself

There is no fixed order. Drag any of the eight items on the left into Require, Optional or Output; anything placed can be moved again or taken out.

  • Drag: items go into the three areas; a placed item can be dragged to another area or group, or back to the library to remove it.
  • Click: And / Or toggles on a click; click a placed item to change its probability or order below the canvas, or to make its group “choose 1 out of N” (clicking the frame of the group does the same).
  • No dragging needed: click an item on the left, then the area it goes to, or use the buttons below the canvas.
Tobie’s note

What creators needed to see was the rule itself: what to hand in, what comes out, which one of several. That is why it is drawn as blocks to move around rather than as a form.

04 · Campaign drafting assistant

Let creators edit a draft instead of facing an empty canvas.

Designed after Studio launched; not shipped.

The freer Studio’s rules became, the harder it was for a creator to start, and the hardest step was the empty canvas. The campaign drafting assistant is a design added for that step: the creator states a goal in one sentence, the assistant drafts a campaign in Studio’s own rule structure (missions, items and recipes), and the creator edits the draft.

The assistant has to hold three constraints. Valid structure: every part of the draft fits an existing Studio field. Craftable: every material a recipe needs can be earned from this campaign’s missions. Back to the home platform: at least half of the missions are completed on the creator’s own platforms.

The creator stays in charge. A draft is never published automatically. Each part explains why it was set up that way, the creator accepts, edits or removes it item by item, and any problem the assistant finds in its own draft is flagged on the draft.

I judge a draft with five checks: valid structure, craftable, back to the home platform, a new fan can start, and fit with the creator’s persona. I prepared three different creator goals, generated one draft for each and checked them line by line: three drafts, fifteen checks, all passed. In the second draft the assistant flagged a problem outside the five checks: only one new-home key is issued, and both recipes need it. This is why a draft goes to the creator first and is never published automatically.

The three drafts below were generated by Claude under these three constraints. The creators, items and campaigns are fictional.

05 · App

Make the cost clear before the fan confirms.

The app redesign started in late October 2023 and took three to four weeks. Crafting changed the most: from a game-like “furnace” to recipe browsing with a consumption check.

Missing materials, requirements met and confirmation are distinct states. Even quick crafting needs to make the consequence clear before the user commits.

Problem
Crafting consumes items and cannot be undone. Recipes from different creators can share inputs but produce different outputs, so fans need to see which recipe applies and what they will give up.
Alternative considered
My first design was a game-like “furnace”: drag materials into a cauldron in the centre of the screen, the recipe fills itself in, and one tap crafts, with an element of surprise.
Why not
The client’s product lead found it too complex. PlayBook is a companion app: claiming and crafting should be as simple as possible, because the goal is to send fans back to the creator’s own platforms. Recipes can also overlap, and a furnace cannot show which one is being used.
Outcome
Crafting moved to one dedicated page, and item pages became a catalogue with a quick-craft entry. Long-pressing a recipe card opens a confirmation that lists the items you will lose and the items you will get. Newer users go through the recipe detail; experienced users take the long-press shortcut. Barter uses the same confirmation.

06 · Context & discovery

Keep community context coherent, but discovery open.

Home, items and missions need to answer the same question: whose community is this? I treated creator selection as shared context so related content remained coherent.

I initially favoured search within a single creator’s world. In the October 2023 product reviews, creator collaboration emerged as a central goal. We moved toward a dedicated global search covering creators, items, recipes and users, retaining local context for everyday tasks.

Tobie’s note

Consistent context helps people orient themselves. A boundary that is too strict can prevent the connections the product needs.

07 · Feedback & collaboration

Small progress should not always interrupt.

In reviews, I argued that routine tasks and significant achievements should not receive equally intrusive feedback. Frequent full-screen dialogs interrupt the experience. Lighter feedback can support everyday progress, while valuable rewards keep an intentional claim step.

Screens, states and interaction demonstrations brought these trade-offs into product discussions and supported product and investor communication. The design made abstract rules concrete enough for the team to examine together.

Problem
In the original UI, “task done” and “reward received” were one state. Returning fans couldn’t tell what was finished and what was still waiting to be claimed, and a long task list on Home buried what mattered.
Alternative considered
Fully automatic: on login, the system marks tasks complete and issues rewards with no tap. I suggested this for daily tasks during a review.
Why not
The client’s product lead wanted fans to tap to collect their rewards. I also argued that rare, long-term tasks only feel earned when fans accept and claim them themselves, while progress on easy tasks changes so often that a dialog every time would only get in the way.
Outcome
Two separate states: completed-but-unclaimed and claimed. Daily tasks are detected automatically and can be claimed one by one or all at once; high-value tasks keep a manual claim and a reward dialog. Home shows only three to five tasks that are in progress or waiting to be claimed, and claimed tasks leave Home. Major progress gets a full-screen dialog; minor progress shows a small “+N” in the top corner.

08 · Collection & showcase

Inventory manages. The showcase expresses.

The original item page tried to manage, craft and display at the same time. I separated them: Inventory answers three questions (what I have, what I’m missing, and how to get it), crafting has its own page, and display belongs to the showcase.

Problem
Home and the profile both had space for displayed items, but the original UI never said where those items were chosen or what appeared when there were none.
Alternative considered
A self-curated trophy cabinet in the style of Sony’s, where fans pick and arrange their own collection.
Why not
The client’s product lead raised the cold-start problem: new fans don’t yet know which items are valuable, so they won’t set up a cabinet on their own.
Outcome
The showcase recommends valuable items from the fan’s inventory and displays them in one tap (“I didn’t know I had this”). It covers four states: empty, choosing from recommendations, filled, and the visitor’s view.

09 · Trading & barter

Buying, selling and swapping all state the cost first.

Besides missions and crafting, fans can buy a missing item in the community or swap spare items for it. I drew about 27 wireframes for the marketplace and barter: market and inventory, listings and buy requests, price trend, listing and purchase confirmation, and posting, accepting or refusing a swap.

After discussions with the client, I wrote the questions I had not yet resolved next to the wireframes (translated from my Chinese notes): “What is barter for in the first place?” “Steam’s trading is one-to-one. Why not one-to-many?” “Do trade and barter orders need a module of their own, or should they live inside messages?” Below the questions I listed three pages: the barter market, my barter requests, and the items I want.

Both flows spell out the cost at the last step. A purchase lists quantity, price and total due before it goes through; a swap separates the items you will lose from the items you will gain, and is only sent after confirmation. This is the same rule crafting follows.

The marketplace and barter flows were reviewed and kept in the design.

10 · Remix

Fans submit. Creators review and collaborate.

Remix is a module in Studio, and I did both its UX and its UI. It does two things: it lets a creator collect ideas from fans, and it lets creators collaborate with one another.

The fan side starts with a challenge. The creator sets up a new challenge with a name and a description, limits the file types and the number of files fans can submit, and sets the timing of each phase and the share that goes to the fan. Fans submit item designs. On the submission page, the creator marks an area of the image and leaves a comment on it, and a side panel keeps each round of feedback by revision. The creator can pick a winner from the challenge page or from the submission page.

The creator side is collaboration. Here a creator sees the items made together with other creators and handles incoming collaboration requests, so that creators can share audiences through joint items.

11 · Outcome & reflection

The team could discuss behaviour, not just screens.

The delivery included Studio UX/UI, App UX flows and states, and demonstration prototypes, and the design was handed over to development.

The client’s founder used the interactive prototypes in investor pitches, and the project secured investment.

If I did it again, I would refine how the two sides, Studio and App, map to each other. Most of my effort went into prototypes. The first app version came quickly, the client wanted something to show investors as soon as possible, and I did not ask for all the information I needed. Communication with the developers also went through the founder.

What I learned: get the main flow right for the main group of users before handling edge cases. We spent a lot of time on cases such as overly long names, and less on the path most fans would take. I also stopped treating wireframes as a rough pass that the UI stage would fix. Rough wireframes leave problems for later.
